strengths: Identifies and addresses a critical limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs), namely the incompleteness of their kernel basis, which limits the expressivity of single convolutional layers.
Provides a mathematically rigorous framework for conditional steerable convolutions, proving the equivariance under input-dependent kernel conditioning.

Maintains computational efficiency by using a translation-invariant conditioning operator (global mean pooling) to enable template matching, avoiding the slow message-passing typical of continuous or point convolutions.

Demonstrates strong and consistent empirical improvements across various physical systems (Navier-Stokes, Shallow-Water, 3D Maxwell, and Relativistic 2D Maxwell), outperforming both standard CSCNNs and several state-of-the-art baselines.
weaknesses: The completeness of the conditional Clifford-Steerable kernel basis (Conjecture 4.1) is not formally proven for the general case of arbitrary pseudo-Euclidean groups, remaining a conjecture with validation limited to the O(2) case and empirical evidence.

The conditioning operator is restricted to global mean pooling in the experiments. While this choice is computationally efficient and mathematically sound, it represents a mean-field approximation that discards local spatial context, which might limit performance in highly non-homogeneous fields.

The explanation of how the angular information propagates through the geometric product of two different multivectors in Section 4.4 relies heavily on SymPy code snippets in the appendix. A more analytical exposition in the main text would strengthen the theoretical presentation.

strengths: Clearly identifies and addresses a critical limitation (kernel incompleteness) of Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs), a recently proposed state-of-the-art framework for pseudo-Euclidean equivariant learning.

The theoretical framework for Conditional Clifford-Steerable CNNs (C-CSCNNs) is well-reasoned and elegant, maintaining rigorous $E(p,q)$ equivariance while introducing input-dependent, more expressive convolutional kernels.

The explanation of how the incompleteness occurs in standard CSCNNs (polar coordinate analysis in $O(2)$) and how the auxiliary input resolves this is highly intuitive and supported by clean symbolic verification (SymPy code in the appendix).

Outstanding empirical results across four diverse and challenging PDE forecasting benchmarks (Navier-Stokes, Shallow-Water, 3D Maxwell, and 2D Relativistic Maxwell). C-CSCNNs consistently outperform standard CSCNNs and other highly competitive baselines (such as Transolver and FNO), demonstrating exceptional data efficiency and scaling properties.
weaknesses: The central claim regarding the 'completeness' of the conditional Clifford-steerable kernel basis remains a conjecture (Conjecture 4.1) for general groups $O(p, q)$, although it is well-supported for the $O(2)$ case.

To maintain computational efficiency, the practical implementation simplifies the general pointwise conditioning framework to a global mean-pooled operator $T$. While effective, this mean-field approximation limits the local expressivity that a fully local conditional convolution could theoretically achieve.
Minor typos are present in the text (e.g., 'The dataset os obtained...' on page 17).

strengths: Identifies a crucial limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs), showing that single-vector inputs restrict the propagation of angular information to grade-1, which leads to an incomplete kernel basis.

Proposes a novel and elegant formulation of Conditional Clifford-Steerable CNNs (C-CSCNNs) by incorporating auxiliary multivector fields into the implicit kernel parameterization, successfully bypassing the incompleteness limit.

Presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation on four different physical PDE systems (Navier-Stokes, Shallow-Water, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic 2D Maxwell), demonstrating substantial performance gains and excellent data efficiency compared to standard CSCNNs and other strong neural operators.

Provides elegant algebraic validation using SymPy in Appendix A.4 and A.5, illustrating clearly how auxiliary multivectors allow the propagation of higher-frequency angular components in the O(2) case.
weaknesses: The central claim of completeness is left as an unproven conjecture. Despite the title claiming a 'Complete Kernel Basis', Conjecture 4.1 is not mathematically proven for the general case. Leaving this central assertion as a conjecture creates a notable gap between the paper's marketing and its concrete theoretical achievements.

Using global mean pooling as the operator T introduces non-local dependencies into the convolutional framework. This shifts the model closer to a mean-field global attention mechanism, which compromises the purely local inductive bias of traditional convolutions. The paper lacks a detailed discussion on how this global coupling affects generalization to larger or differently shaped domains.

There is no detailed analysis of computational efficiency or latency. Although the authors state that the cost of global pooling is negligible, the kernel network must now ingest a larger input dimension (the concatenated relative position and auxiliary multivector stack). Quantitative evidence of wall-clock training/inference times and memory usage compared to standard CSCNNs is missing.

The translation invariance of the global mean pooling operator on bounded domains is not thoroughly discussed. While Appendix B introduces circular masking to prevent boundary effects from breaking rotation equivariance, the implications of boundaries on the translation and rotation equivariance of the global conditioning vector warrant further clarification.

strengths: Identifies and successfully resolves a major limitation (kernel incompleteness) of the recently proposed Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs).
Provides a sound mathematical formulation, including proofs of equivariance for the conditional convolutions under pseudo-Euclidean groups E(p, q).

Demonstrates excellent empirical results on multiple physical forecasting tasks (Navier-Stokes, Shallow-water, Maxwell), consistently outperforming standard CSCNNs and showing competitiveness against advanced transformer-based PDE solvers.
The proposed conditioning mechanism (e.g., using mean-pooled multivectors) is simple and elegant, introducing negligible computational overhead compared to the standard CSCNN baseline.
weaknesses: The completeness of the conditional kernel basis is only proved for the O(2, 0) group, whereas for general O(p, q) groups it remains a conjecture (Conjecture 4.7).
The investigation of conditional operators is limited to very simple choices (mean/max pooling), leaving more expressive localized conditioning operators for future work.

Although the conditioning adds minimal overhead to standard CSCNNs, the overall family of Clifford-based convolutions remains computationally expensive compared to standard CNNs and some transformer alternatives.

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical foundation: The authors identify a concrete and significant limitation of standard Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs)—specifically, the incompleteness of the kernel basis (e.g., missing frequency-2 components)—and provide an elegant solution to address it.

Mathematical rigor: The paper mathematically derives the steerability constraints for conditional kernels and proves that the proposed formulation maintains exact pseudo-Euclidean equivariance. Clear and reproducible algebraic derivations (using SymPy) are included in the appendix to illustrate how the conditioning restores completeness in the O(2) case.

Computational efficiency: By utilizing a translation-invariant conditioning operator (like mean/max pooling), the framework avoids the computationally expensive message-passing formulation, enabling efficient parallel computation. The empirical timing results demonstrate that the conditioning mechanism introduces negligible overhead (under 1%).

Strong empirical results: The proposed C-CSCNN model consistently and significantly outperforms the standard CSCNN baseline across various physical simulation tasks (Navier-Stokes, Shallow-Water, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic 2D Maxwell) and matches or exceeds state-of-the-art architectures like Transolver and CViT under fair parameter-matching settings.
weaknesses: Completeness is left as a conjecture: Although the authors prove completeness of the kernel basis for $O(2,0)$ and provide strong empirical evidence for higher dimensions, Conjecture 4.7 remains unproven for arbitrary $O(p, q)$.

Simplistic conditioning operator: The current design relies on simple spatial pooling (mean/max) for the conditioning operator $T$. While computationally light and effective, this global mean-field approximation may underperform in modeling highly non-local interactions compared to attention-based mechanisms (such as Transolver in the electrodynamics tasks).

Reliance on standard CNN backbones: The current implementation is built on a ResNet architecture. Exploring more modern and expressive backbones like ConvNeXt or Transformers integrated with Clifford-steerable conditional kernels could further unlock the potential of this method.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs), namely the incompleteness of the implicit kernel basis, which previously required parameter-doubling workarounds.

Provides a mathematically rigorous framework for conditional steerable convolutions, proving the necessary G-equivariance constraints (Lemma 4.2) and establishing how to maintain E(p,q)-equivariance using translation-invariant operators (Proposition 4.5).

Presents an elegant and computationally efficient solution using equivariant global mean pooling, which introduces virtually no inference overhead (less than 1%) while dramatically improving expressivity.

Exhibits highly thorough empirical evaluation across four diverse PDE modeling tasks (Navier-Stokes, Shallow-Water, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic 2D Maxwell), demonstrating substantial and consistent performance gains over standard CSCNNs and matching or exceeding other SOTA baselines.
The paper is very well-written, with clear explanations, illustrative figures, and self-contained proofs and symbolic verification code in the appendix.
weaknesses: The choice of the conditioning operator $T$ is mostly restricted to global mean pooling. While equivariant and efficient, global pooling collapses all spatial variation, which may limit performance on highly non-local or heterogeneous physical systems.
The completeness of the conditional kernel basis is proved for $O(2,0)$ but remains a conjecture (Conjecture 4.7) for arbitrary pseudo-Euclidean groups $O(p,q)$, leaving a theoretical gap.

The mechanism of recovering high-frequency components relies on multiple layers of geometric products within the implicit kernel network. The paper would benefit from a clearer discussion or analysis of how the depth/capacity of the kernel network quantitatively scales with the maximum frequency representation.
